newsitem.title: JAPAN: Hokkaido banks say merger on track despite reports.
newsitem.headline: Hokkaido banks say merger on track despite reports.

text.p: Former rivals Hokkaido Bank Ltd and Hokkaido Takushoku Bank Ltd gave assurances on Thursday that there would be no delay in their merger set for next April, dampening speculation that a dispute over problem loans could end the engagement.

Despite media reports that the merger would be postponed, the banks said that they would come up with a programme by the end of September to rationalise their businesses, a major step towards proceeding with the merger as scheduled.
"We are not considering delaying the merger," Hokkaido Bank President Tsuneo Fujita told Reuters.
"It is true that a problem remains over how to deal with problem loans, but it is not true that we are considering postponing the planned merger with Takushoku Bank," he said.

The business daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun reported on Thursday that the two banks were at odds over their evaluation of the amount of problem loans at Hokkaido Takushoku Bank, with Hokkaido Bank believing that Hokkaido Takushoku has underestimated the amount of its problem loans.
Fujita added that, while he has repeatedly said that devising a rationalisation plan will not be an easy task, it does not mean that the two have started to consider delaying the merger.
An official at Hokkaido Takushoku also said that the two banks have continued to talk about various aspects of the merger, such as employee pay scales.
"It is not true that we are considering delaying the planned merger at a time when we continue discussions on the merger," he said.
In a bid to move the process along, both banks have agreed to allow the other's accounting firm to examine the accuracy of their problem loan assessments, he added.

In April, Hokkaido Takushoku, Japan's 10th-largest commercial bank, said it and the smaller Hokkaido Bank would merge as equals. Both banks are based in Sapporo, the largest city on Japan's northernmost island of Hokkaido.
The announcement surprised the financial markets as Hokkaido Bank had been a major competitor of Hokkaido Takushoku in the region.

Despite the denials, financial analysts and industry sources see a rift growing between the two troubled banks, which are both saddled with problem loans, and say that this issue may ultimately affect the fate of the merger.
"Hokkaido Takushoku did not know Hokkaido Bank held a meeting for analysts yesterday. This is a minor example but I see a rift growing between them over this," one analyst said.
The two banks are competing with each other to take the leading role in the planned merger, and Hokkaido Bank might be unhappy as the merger ratio is on an equal basis, he said.

Analysts said that the merger is vital for Hokkaido Takushoku, which has long been considered the most troubled of Japan's major city banks, burdened with bad loans after Japan's bubble of inflated asset prices burst in the early 1990s.

Hokkaido Takushoku has forecast 3.0 billion yen ($25.8 million) in parent current profits for the 1997/98 business year ending in March, but analysts say the bank may post losses if Tokyo share prices fall and it is forced to dispose aggressively of problem loans.

On Thursday, after the newspaper report of the possible delay in the planned merger, shares in Hokkaido Takushoku fell three yen to end at 114 yen, while Hokkaido Bank's shares closed up two yen at 138 yen.
